6	# Chosing models
7	
8	## Goal
9	Someone running a feature through the agent decides which model does which work: one profile per phase of that feature's plan — blind plan, map against code, implement — and one profile per chat session, switchable while the session is in play. Today the model comes from settings alone, so whatever plans also implements, and the choice is invisible where the work happens. Making it part of the plan lets the strongest reasoner plan and a cheaper, faster model carry out the tasks, and lets a chat move to another model without losing the conversation. The two choices are independent: what a plan's phases run on says nothing about what a chat runs on.
10	
11	## Choosing a model for each phase of a plan
12	The user picks, per feature, which configured profile each phase runs on, before or while the feature is being worked.
13	
14	- **B1**: each phase of a feature that runs a model — blind plan, map against code, implement — carries its own profile choice, picked from the configured profiles; verification runs no model and takes no choice. (docs/intent/agent.md#Per-phase model)
15	- **B2**: a phase with no choice runs on the settings default — the plan profile for the blind plan, the active profile otherwise — so a feature nobody chose for runs exactly as it does today.
16	- **B3**: a choice takes effect on the next turn of that phase; a turn already in flight finishes on the model it started on, and a phase that already ended is not re-run by the choice.
17	  - **E1**: the implement phase's profile is changed while the board is part-worked → the next implement turn runs on the new profile and the existing task markers stand.
18	- **B4**: a phase that would continue the conversation of the phase before it does so only when its chosen profile runs on the same engine; on a different engine it starts fresh, carrying the conversation it had. (docs/intent/agent.md#Shape)
19	- **B5**: a retrieval sub-session keeps its own profile and is unaffected by the choice made for the phase that called it. (docs/intent/agent.md#Retrieval)
20	- **B6**: a choice naming a profile that is no longer configured falls back to the settings default and says so, rather than refusing to run the phase.
21	- **B7**: the choices are held per feature and per user, outside the spec and the tasks file, so they never change the feature's derived stage and never make a mapped board stale.
22	- **B8**: the plan view shows, for each phase, the profile it will run on, including when that profile is the settings default.
23	
24	## Switching model in a chat session
25	A chat session runs on one profile at a time and the user can change it mid-conversation.
26	
27	- **B9**: a chat session has its own profile, independent of any feature's phase choices, switchable from the composer at any point while the session is in play. (docs/intent/agent.md#Engines)
28	  - **E2**: a plan session's composer shows the profile its current phase runs on and offers no switch there — a plan's model is chosen per phase.
29	- **B10**: a switch takes effect on the next prompt; a turn in flight finishes on the model it started on.
30	- **B11**: after a switch the session carries on with the conversation it already has rather than starting over; nothing that only the previous engine held is carried.
31	- **B12**: a new chat session starts on the active-profile setting, and switching changes that session only — not the setting and not other sessions.
32	- **B13**: the composer shows which profile the session is on, and the transcript records each switch where it happened, so a reader can tell which model produced which part of the conversation.

1	# Agent definition
2	
3	## Why
4	
5	Blind planning exists because a planner that can read the code inherits the code's mistakes as constraints. Every workaround becomes an implicit requirement, and the feature gets shaped to fit the defect. Deriving the spec from intent alone makes disagreement between intent and implementation visible rather than silently absorbed. Phase 2 is not "soften the spec until it fits"; it is "name each disagreement and rule on it", with the code as the presumed-wrong party.
6	
7	## Engines
8	
9	A session runs on one engine, chosen per session or per phase:
10	
11	- Claude through the Agent SDK (Claude Code as a library, JavaScript build, inherited Claude Code login).
12	- Any OpenAI-compatible provider (Berget AI's GLM and Kimi, say) with our own loop and tools.
13	
14	The extension only sees `CodeSession`: send a prompt, stream events, answer permission requests, interrupt. Engines differ below that line.
15	
16	Both take the workspace's `.mcp.json`: Claude through its own MCP client, the own loop through a client per server. The tools carry the same names and fall under the same permission rules on either engine, so a project's servers work the same whichever model runs.
17	
18	## Shape
19	
20	Three phases, each a session with its own system prompt and tool set. The state is files on disk: a phase can always start from them. Blindness is the boundary: nothing that has seen the code reaches the plan session as conversation. Below it a re-check continues the last check's conversation where the engine resumes, so what was read is not read again. Implementation does not continue a conversation: each task is built by a run of its own, started on the board's hand-off, and the cleanup run starts on its size report. Planning produces the spec; approving it hands it to the build. The check against the code runs between the two and speaks up only when the code disagrees: its decisions go into a file of their own, never into the spec.
21	
22	```
23	docs/**  +  specs  +  work item  →  spec.md  →  approved spec  →  decisions.md  →  revised spec  →  tasks.json  →  code  →  tests pass
24	                                   (blind)                        (check code)     (rulings)        (derived)     (implement)  (verification)
25	```
26	
27	An approved spec is the feature's definition: rules and edge cases in the product's language, ruled by the user, with no path or symbol in it. The next feature is planned from the specs as much as from the docs, so what one feature settled reaches the next without a step of its own.
28	
29	Nothing in the plan files is a synthetic id. A rule, a task and a decision are named, the way a test or a function is named, and the name is the anchor everything else refers to: a comment names the rule it is on, a task names the rules it delivers, a proof names the rule a test proves, a decision names the rules it concerns. Names are stable; a rename carries a `(was Old name)` note the extension follows through every file.
30	
31	### Stages
32	
33	Where a feature stands is derived from its files and held nowhere else, so the stage and the files can never disagree. The spec is committed under `plan/`; the review, decisions and tasks are working files under `.agent/plan/`, never committed. A week after they were last touched, the working files of a verified feature or of a spec that is gone are deleted when the extension starts, and a verified feature's spec is marked `status: implemented` first, so its stage outlives them. The plan view adapts to it. One row is the plan bar: the steps (Plan, Review, Approve, Rule, Implement, Verify) with the one the stage asks of the person lit, Rule shown only when the check found something, and at its right the one next thing: a button when it moves the plan on (Submit review, Approve, Send rulings, Implement, Verify), a link into the plan when the act is on a row there (answers to resolve, decisions to rule on), a line of text while the planner or a run is at work. Nothing restates the stage in words. The row under it is one strip of tabs: the plan's, each present once it has content (Spec with the goal, scenarios and questions commented on in place; Review with the rounds, the planner's answers and Resolve; Decisions, one at a time; Tasks), and Chat last. A reached step opens the tab it works in; Review stays reachable on any draft, nothing past approval.
34	
35	| stage | derived from |
36	|---|---|
37	| created | spec is `draft`, no review in flight |
38	| under review | comments or strikes are being written, or the planner has yet to answer them |
39	| final draft | every comment is answered; the human reads the revised spec and accepts, or comments again |
40	| checking | approved, no board yet, no decision pending: the check runs, or the planner applies rulings |
41	| ruling | approved, no board yet, a decision is pending |
42	| under development | approved, the board exists, not every task tested |
43	| verification | every task tested; the test commands have yet to pass |
44	| verified | every task tested and the last recorded run passed, or the spec is `implemented` |
45	
46	Approve is offered on a draft with no open comment. Approving starts the check against the code by itself.
47	
48	A session that is picked up after its engine stopped is set up afresh: it carries the conversation it had, and the instructions and generated context a session starting now would get.
49	
50	## Phase 1: Blind plan
51	
52	Sees: feature description, domain brief (ubiquitous language, stack, constraints), `docs/**`, the workspace README, every feature's spec under `plan/*.spec.md`, the unfiled decisions, the docs map, one work item closure when ADO is connected.
53	Never sees: source, PRs, build output, generated context drawn from the code such as the repo map, another feature's review, tasks or decisions. The docs map is the exception that proves the rule: generated, but from the docs alone, so it carries nothing the planner could not read itself.
54	
55	Until ADO is connected the feature description is typed by the user or picked from the docs. The agent plans the user story itself; the tasks file is the source for the ADO tasks created under the story once ADO is connected (write-back, not read-only).
56	
57	Tools: Read/Glob/MarkdownSearch scoped to `docs/**`, the workspace README, the specs and the feature's own plan files, `get_work_item(id)`, AskUserQuestion, optionally WebSearch. Bash denied by bare name (allow-lists only auto-approve; a bare-name deny removes the tool from context). A write into `docs/**` is neither the phase's deliverable nor off limits: it goes through the permission prompt, and the planner makes one only when the user asks.
58	
59	First a direction in chat (the decisions that shape the feature, the questions that would change them); nothing is written until the user says go. Then `plan/<feature>.spec.md`, to the contract below. A rule derived from a doc or another spec ends with a citation of its section (`(docs/intent/orders.md#Cancellation)`, `(plan/orders.spec.md#Cancelling an order)`); an uncited rule is the planner's default. An approved spec weighs as a doc; a draft is a proposal still being planned. Where a doc and an approved spec disagree, the planner asks: the user knows which is current. To the point, not complete: a rule earns its place by changing what gets built or how it is tested. No code paths. If neither the docs nor the specs have anything on the feature, ask and stop.
60	
61	### The spec contract
62	
63	```markdown
64	## Goal
65	Prose.
66	
67	## Cancelling an order            ← a scenario: a situation from the user's side
68	- **Cancel command**: a rule, written so a test can prove it (docs/intent/orders.md#Cancellation)
69	  - **Shipped order**: situation → outcome, an edge of the rule above
70	- **Refund on cancel**: another rule
71	
72	## Open questions
73	- **Partial refunds**: what only the user can settle
74	```
75	
76	`Goal` and `Open questions` are reserved; every other `##` is a scenario, and a small feature has one. Rules sit directly under a scenario; an edge case is nested under the rule it qualifies, one level, no deeper. Every rule, edge case and question is named by the bold lead-in of its line, unique in the spec; the name never changes once written, a rename carries `(was Old name)` after the new one. There are no invariants, acceptance criteria or task sections: an invariant is a rule, an acceptance criterion restates one, and the evidence that a rule holds is the test the implementer names for it. The extension parses the spec into this model on every write and hands what does not fit back to the model on the same tool result; the plan view shows the problems and offers Repair, which runs the migration (below) for that plan.
77	
78	### get_work_item
79	
80	Hand-coded, read-only, Azure DevOps. Server-side filtering is the enforcement.
81	
82	- Include: title, description, parent chain, Goal/Actor/Impact/Behaviour/Example.
83	- Exclude: state, comments, tasks, linked PRs/commits/branches/builds, `System.*` and `Microsoft.VSTS.*` fields.
84	- Walks parents, children, related. Depth and total caps, cycle detection, deterministic ordering. Returns markdown. Snapshot to `plan/<feature>.context.md`.
85	- State is excluded deliberately: a Done item over drifted code is evidence for phase 2, not input to phase 1.
86	- Prose may leak file paths; accepted, or stripped in the tool.
87	
88	### Docs split
89	
90	The whole of `docs/**` and every spec is phase 1 scope. What phase 1 is kept from is the code and what travels with it: source, PRs, build output, generated context, the check's files. Those drift with the code in the same direction and arrive labelled as authority.
91	
92	`docs/**` holds what no spec holds: the domain brief, the constraints, the features not yet planned. Once a spec is approved it is the feature's definition, and the doc it was planned from may say less, or otherwise. Nobody trims that by hand unprompted, so once the check against the code comes back clean the plan session lists in chat, per doc section, what now reads differently from the spec or is covered by it and can go. The user edits, or tells the planner to, and each of its writes into `docs/**` is confirmed.
93	
94	### Finding the way in
95	
96	Scope is not the same as access. A planner that may read everything under `docs/**` still has to guess which file holds the answer, and reads whole documents to find a paragraph. So it starts with the docs map: every doc, what it is for, and one line per heading. Generated context, like the repo map, and blind-safe because it is derived from the docs and nothing else. It also fixes the citations: a rule cites `path#Heading`, and the map spells every heading out, so the planner cites what exists rather than what it remembers reading.
97	
98	Inside a doc, every session reads by section. The first whole-file Read of a markdown doc over 200 lines in a session answers with its outline (headings with line spans) instead; a second whole-file Read goes through. MarkdownSearch returns each match with its closest heading as `path#Heading` and that section's span, and returns nothing from a file the session may not read. Plan files are exempt from the outline, and so is the docs-map run, which describes every section.
99	
100	How the docs are arranged is therefore part of how well the product can be planned, and it is nobody's job by default. The docs evaluation is that job: a session with the planner's own read scope that says where the arrangement costs a planner, and changes the docs when the user says which. Work past the docs, such as moving files out of `docs/`, is done by continuing the evaluation in chat, which carries its conversation on with the full tool set. It judges discovery, never correctness: whether the docs are right is settled against the code, in phase 2, on one feature at a time.
101	
102	## Phase 2: Check against code
103	
104	Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, JsonSchema, JsonQuery, MarkdownSearch, Skill; Edit and Write on the feature's decisions file only. The spec is never the check's to write. Bash denied by bare name.
105	Input: spec + context + repo, the agent's own generated files included: what a build wrote for the run to use is part of what it may read. Not the phase 1 transcript, and not `docs/**` or the other specs: the spec is the intent for this feature, and the citations on its rules are what the check opens when it needs intent's exact words.
106	
107	A run, not a session: started by Approve, it runs under the plan session's tab with no tab or transcript of its own, only a one-line progress indicator in the plan bar and a stop. It ends when its turn ends; a re-check is a new run. Its full transcript is in the run log for inspection.
108	
109	The job is to find what stands in the feature's way before any code is written, not to grade the spec. It runs before the build rather than inside it because a conflict found halfway can undo the tasks before it, and because a run whose job is to finish is pulled toward absorbing the defect it should report. Only disagreements are reported, each as a decision for the user; a rule the code accommodates without incident is not mentioned. An empty list is a valid result, and the build starts on it without the person being asked anything. What the run looks for: a business rule in the code that says otherwise (the human decides which side is right), existing behaviour the feature would change or break that the spec does not mention, and something the spec assumes that the code shows to be wrong. Only in code the feature will change or build on: behaviour in code the feature leaves alone is not a finding. Where the feature is built, when that is open, is one decision ruled before the findings it would make moot. A constraint on how a rule is built rather than what it does is not a decision: the implementer reads the same code.
110	
111	Output: `.agent/plan/<feature>.decisions.md`, one `###` per decision titled by the disagreement, with an `on` line naming the rules it concerns and a `finding` line of one or two sentences: what the code does, at the one path and symbol that shows it, and what the spec says; not how it was found and not what the spec should say instead. The run writes titles, `on` and `finding` only. When the run ends with decisions that have no proposal, the plan session is handed their titles and adds one to three `proposed` lines under each: distinct ways to settle it, each the rule's new text as it would stand in the spec: observable behaviour, not how it is built. Keeping the rule is not proposed; it is always offered.
112	
113	```markdown
114	### Shipped orders cannot be cancelled
115	- on: Cancel command
116	- finding: what the code does, at one path and symbol, and what the spec says
117	- proposed: the rule's new text, one way
118	- proposed: the rule's new text, another way
119	- ruling: keep
120	```
121	
122	Findings are a temporal state: the spec never holds one, so a later planner reads rules, not paths. The user rules in a wizard on the plan view's Decisions tab, one decision at a time, the finding explained and the ways to settle it as buttons: change the spec one of the proposed ways, keep the spec (the code changes), or an own ruling in the user's words. A pick writes the `ruling` line and moves on to the next open decision; nothing is sent. Send rulings, from the plan bar, needs every decision ruled (with several options there is no default) and hands the rulings to the plan session, which revises the rules per each ruling (a proposal's text replaces the rule verbatim, so the rule stays one sentence; `keep` moves nothing; own words are worked into the rules) and marks the decision `[applied]`. The spec is approved by then; a ruling amends it without a second approval, since the ruling is the person's own. When the planner's turn ends with every decision applied, the check runs again, continuing its conversation, since a revised rule can meet the code anew. A `keep` ruling is settled work: the re-check reports the finding no more, and the finding reaches the implementer on the task that delivers a rule it is `on`. When a plan turn ends, each applied decision is cut to its `on`, finding and ruling: the spec holds the outcome, and the proposals are read by no one. A decision the check finds no longer holds on a re-run is marked `[withdrawn]`.
123	
124	Once a check ends with no decision pending, the extension derives the task board, `.agent/plan/<feature>.tasks.json`, from the spec: one task per scenario, named and grouped by the scenario's title, delivering its rules and edge cases, so every rule is delivered by construction. The implementer fills in the files it touches. A task is re-derived by its name whenever the spec changes under the board, keeping the implementer's progress; a scenario gone from the spec leaves its task marked removed. The board records the fingerprint of the spec it was derived from. The docs listing (see Docs split) runs then, on the spec as ruled, and the build starts. The plan view's Tasks tab shows the scenario, each task's state and its files.
125	
126	A board mapped by an earlier version of the extension carries `context` and `how` from the mapping run; they stay readable and reach the implementer as before.
127	
128	Authority order is fixed in the prompt: work item, then the docs and the approved specs, then code. What a ruling settles reaches the next feature's planner through the approved spec, which it reads; what the docs then say wrongly or twice is listed once the check is clean (see Docs split).
129	
130	### The check has no voice
131	
132	The check has no conversation of its own: while it works, the person sees a single line of progress on the plan it runs under. What it cannot settle it writes down as a finding for the person to rule on, and never asks.
133	
134	## Retrieval
135	
136	A sub-session the planner calls with `retrieve(question, known, budget)` to keep file dumps out of its own context. Phase 2 first; phase 1 only when the intent tree or work-item graph outgrows the planner.
137	
138	- Locates and quotes, never interprets. Output is verbatim excerpts with provenance; the planner rules on them. A summary drops nuance silently, and the planner never sees what was left out.
139	- Tools are derived, not configured: the calling phase's tool set minus AskUserQuestion and anything that writes. Phase 1 retrieval is blind by construction.
140	- No user interaction, no recursion. "Needs X to answer" goes in `not_found`; the planner decides whether to ask. Depth 1.
141	- Result: `findings[]` (excerpt, source as `path#heading`, work item id or URL, one line on why it matches), `not_found[]` (what was looked for, where), `status: complete | partial | budget_exhausted`. Partial is a result, not an error.
142	- Written to `.agent/runs/<id>/retrieval/<n>.md`; the tool returns path, status and counts. Files on disk, not conversation context.
143	- Budget per call (tool calls, tokens), set by the planner. Exhaustion returns findings so far.
144	- Runs as a `CodeSession` under its own profile; a cheap model is fine because the task is search.
145	- Independent questions fan out as independent sessions, no shared state.
146	
147	## Phase 3: Implement
148	
149	Tools: Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep, JsonSchema, JsonQuery, MarkdownSearch, Bash, ReadTasks, UpdateTask. Input is the approved spec and its task board; refuses to start on `status: draft` or without a tasks file. One run per task, under the plan's tab, started by the extension on the next unfinished task and closed once that task is tested or blocked, when the next one's run starts. A run starts on its task in full, the text of the rules it delivers and what earlier tasks built, so it never inherits a context filled with finished work, and its system prompt is the same for every task, so each run after the first starts on a cached prefix. A task whose run stopped unfinished is carried on by that run. A failed test sweep goes to a fix run of its own, started on the failure and the tasks it names. A decision ruled `keep` reaches it in the kickoff of the task that delivers a rule the decision is `on`: the spec stands, the code changes. A fork the spec and the code leave open is put to the user with AskUser and the run carries on with the answer. An answer on a rule the task delivers amends the spec under the contract, and the board is derived again when the run's turn ends, without a check: the run has read the code. An answer that reaches further is an unfiled decision. Writes go through the ordinary permission prompt; no scope guard. An implement session may write anywhere the user allows, generated files included: what protects generated output is that the next build rewrites it wholesale, so an edit into it is lost, not refused.
150	
151	- Task state is the board, read with `ReadTasks` and moved with `UpdateTask`: the extension marks a task in progress when its run starts, and the run records how it ended, tested when every rule the task delivers is proven by a passing test, blocked with a reason when it cannot finish, done when it must stop with the code written but untested. A tested task says what it `built`, by name and file: the hand-off the tasks after it start from. The task names every file it touched: the sweep runs over them, so tested is refused on a task that names none. The board file itself is denied to the implementer's Write and Edit.
152	- Coverage is the evidence: the task's proofs name, per delivered rule, the test file and the test whose name states the rule. The plan view shows on each rule and edge case which task delivers it and which test proves it, or `no task` / `no test`; a task marked tested with a rule it names no test for is flagged. That is what an acceptance section used to promise, made checkable.
153	- Only tested is a finish. A board whose every task is tested goes to verification; the plan bar stops offering Implement, since a second session would re-read the code and decide for itself what to redo. Blocked is unfinished work, so it still takes a fresh session. The feature's state is derived from the task states, not a `status` of its own: adding a task to a finished board makes it unfinished again with nothing to reset, and the two can never disagree.
154	
155	## Unfiled decisions
156	
157	A decision the user makes outside planning, one a blind planner could otherwise decide differently, is intent the planner cannot see. The session that hears it records it where the planner reads. Within the task being built, it amends the spec. Reaching further, from an implement run, a plan session or a chat, it becomes an entry in `plan/unfiled-decisions.md`: committed, readable in phase 1, and outweighing a doc or spec that says otherwise. Written in the product's language, never a path or a symbol. *File decisions* is a session with the planner's read scope that moves each entry into the specs and docs it names, each write confirmed, and deletes it once filed; an implemented spec is not amended, since the change is a feature to plan. The pick-up menu shows how many entries wait.
158	
159	## Migration
160	
161	`KiwiAgent: Migrate plans` brings every plan under `plan/` to the contract; Repair in the plan bar does it for one. I read the spec (`plan/chosing-models.spec.md`) and its citations in `docs/intent/agent.md` and `docs/settings.md`, then checked the existing model/profile machinery (`src/agent/session/model-profile.ts`, `src/agent/session/session-manager.ts`, `src/extension.ts`, `src/settings/*`, `src/chat/chat-view-provider.ts`, `src/chat/webview/chat-composer.ts`, `src/chat/webview/chat-transcript.ts`).

Much of the spec already matches current behaviour (same-engine-only conversation continuation, per-session `setProfile` leaving the default setting untouched, the composer already hiding the model switch outside chat mode), so those aren't reported. Four disagreements went into `.agent/plan/chosing-models.decisions.md`:

- **Cleanup is a feature-scoped model phase B1 leaves out** — cleanup already gets its own configured model today, same as plan/reconcile/implement, but B1 doesn't name it among the per-feature choosable phases.
- **Cross-engine handoff does not carry the conversation** — switching engines today drops the conversation entirely rather than carrying it forward, contradicting B4 and B11.
- **Missing-provider is refused, not a settings-default fallback** — `resolveStep` deliberately hard-refuses on a missing provider, the opposite of B6's fallback-and-say-so policy for a stale choice.
- **The transcript shows only the current model, not where it changed** — the status line is overwritten in place, so B13's "tell which model produced which part" isn't achievable as built.
